title: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors — worked eigenvector problems
summary: Three class eigenvalue/eigenvector problems. Exact textbook matches link to the verified textbook-question solution instead of duplicating a second solution; a near-match is identified without inventing missing class working.
transcription_policy: Notebook question data and visible slips are preserved. Before any independent solution is added, each class question is checked against the prescribed textbook worked examples and in-scope question sets. Exact matches link to the textbook anchor instead of duplicating a solution; near-matches state the differing data and link only for comparison.

items.title: Example 3 — Find the eigenvalues and corresponding eigenvectors

math_mismatch.label: Notebook mismatch
math_mismatch.message: In the handwritten final summary for \(\lambda=3\), the third entry of the eigenvector appears without the minus sign. Direct substitution shows that \([2,1,2]^T\) is not an eigenvector for \(\lambda=3\); the verified vector is \([2,1,-2]^T\) (or any non-zero scalar multiple).

textbook_match.label: Exact textbook match
textbook_match.note: The class matrix is exactly Grewal Problems 2.9 Q3(b). Use the single verified textbook solution rather than maintaining a duplicate class solution.

items.title: Example 4 — Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors

math_mismatch.label: Notebook mismatch
math_mismatch.message: The notebook briefly lists the roots as \(8,6,2\) and starts a \(\lambda=6\) case. But its own characteristic polynomial factors as \(-(\lambda-8)(\lambda-2)^2\). Therefore \(6\) is not an eigenvalue; the correct eigenvalues are \(8,2,2\).

textbook_match.label: Exact textbook match
textbook_match.note: The class matrix is exactly Grewal Problems 2.9 Q3(e). Use the textbook-question solution; the notebook root slip is still noted below.

items.title: Example 5 — Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors

math_mismatch.label: Notebook mismatch
math_mismatch.message: In the handwritten determinant setup, the top-left entry is written as \(-2\). In \(A-\lambda I\), \(\lambda\) must be subtracted from every diagonal entry, so that entry should be \(-2-\lambda\). The photographed notes stop during this setup. No independently invented continuation is retained.

textbook_match.label: Near textbook match
textbook_match.note: The class matrix has +2 in position (3,2), while Grewal Q3(d) has −2 there. Because one sign changes the eigenproblem, this is not treated as the same question.

source_notes: The source consists of seven notebook photographs: Mac-class-unit2 - 5.jpg through Mac-class-unit2 - 11.jpg; raw notebook images are not copied into website assets.
The top of page 5 is the tail end of the 8 September property example. The dated 9 September work begins at Example 3 below the written date.
Before adding any completion, all three class questions were compared with the prescribed Grewal Unit II worked examples and in-scope question sets.

Example 3 exactly matches Problems 2.9 Q3(b), and Example 4 exactly matches Problems 2.9 Q3(e); both now link to those anchored textbook questions instead of duplicating independently generated solutions.

Example 5 is only a near-match to Problems 2.9 Q3(d): the class matrix has +2 in entry (3,2), whereas the textbook has -2. The photographed class notes stop during the determinant setup, so no invented continuation is retained.
